In Japan, public bathhouses, known as sento, were once a central part of everyday life in neighborhoods. Before most homes had their own bathrooms, people visited them regularly to wash and to talk with neighbors. However, the number of sento has declined sharply over the past several decades. Rising costs for fuel and water, along with the spread of private bathrooms, have forced many owners to close their businesses. Today, only a small fraction of the bathhouses that existed in the 1960s remain in operation.

Supporters of these bathhouses argue that they deserve to be preserved as cultural assets. Many sento have decorative tile murals, wooden lockers, and architecture that reflects the design styles of their era, and some are registered as cultural properties by local governments. In addition, bathhouses have begun to attract visitors from abroad who are interested in traditional Japanese customs. Some operators have introduced new services, such as cafés and community events, to bring in younger customers and help sustain their businesses.

Nevertheless, keeping these facilities open is far from easy. Many sento are run by elderly owners who have no successors, and the buildings themselves are often old and expensive to repair. Some residents also feel uncomfortable sharing a bath with strangers, and the younger generation tends to prefer modern facilities. As a result, many experts believe that without financial support from local governments, more bathhouses will disappear in the coming years, taking with them a part of the country's shared history.

In recent years, wearable devices that monitor sleep have become popular among people who want to improve their health. These gadgets, which are often worn on the wrist or placed under a mattress, record how long a person sleeps, how often they wake up during the night, and how much time they spend in deep sleep. The data is then displayed on a smartphone app, which may offer advice on bedtime routines or caffeine intake. Sales of these products have risen rapidly in many countries.

Users say that the devices have encouraged them to take sleep more seriously. Many people who had never considered their sleep habits now go to bed at a regular time and avoid using screens before bedtime. Some doctors also see potential benefits, since long-term records of sleep patterns could help identify problems such as sleep apnea or insomnia at an earlier stage. Researchers are studying whether the information gathered by these devices could support the diagnosis of certain conditions.

However, medical experts warn that the results are not always accurate. Consumer devices measure movement and heart rate rather than brain activity, so their estimates of sleep stages can differ from those obtained in a sleep laboratory. Some users also become anxious about small changes in their scores, which can make it harder to fall asleep. In addition, the personal health data collected by these companies raises concerns about privacy, since it is not always clear how it is stored or shared with third parties.

Between the late 1990s and the 2010s, Japan carried out a major wave of municipal mergers, in which neighboring towns and villages combined to form larger cities. The national government encouraged the process with financial incentives, and the number of municipalities fell from more than 3,200 to around 1,700. The main motive was the decline in population. As young people moved to large cities, many small local governments struggled to pay for schools, roads, and welfare services with a shrinking tax base.

Supporters argue that mergers make local government more efficient. Combining administrative offices and sharing staff can reduce costs, and a larger city may be able to employ specialists in areas such as disaster prevention, urban planning, and elderly care. Some merged cities have also coordinated bus routes and waste collection across a wider area, which removes duplicated work. Proponents therefore claim that larger units are better equipped to deliver stable services in an era of population decline.

However, the savings promised by mergers have often been smaller than expected. Integrating computer systems, harmonizing fees, and building new facilities can be expensive, and the financial benefits may not appear for many years. Critics also warn that residents of former villages may feel ignored by a distant town hall. Local festivals and community traditions can weaken, and people in remote areas may find it harder to reach public offices. For these reasons, many researchers argue that mergers should be judged by whether services remain adequate for every resident, not by budget figures alone.

As global temperatures rise, many large cities are experiencing more frequent and severe heat waves. Concrete, asphalt, and glass absorb and retain heat, so urban areas are often several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside. This phenomenon, known as the urban heat island effect, can increase energy demand for air conditioning and pose serious health risks for elderly residents. In response, a growing number of city governments have started large-scale tree-planting programs.

Trees cool the environment in several ways. Their leaves provide shade, and through a process called transpiration they release water vapor that lowers the temperature of the surrounding air. Studies have shown that streets lined with trees can be noticeably cooler than those without them. Trees also absorb carbon dioxide and filter pollutants from the air, and they can reduce the amount of rainwater that flows into drains during heavy storms. Many residents also report that green spaces improve their mood.

Nevertheless, planting trees in cities presents practical difficulties. Urban soil is often compacted and polluted, and young trees need regular watering, which requires money and labor. Underground pipes and power lines can also limit where trees can be planted. Moreover, some residents worry that large trees may block sunlight or damage buildings. Because of these challenges, experts stress that tree planting must be carefully planned and maintained over many years if it is to succeed.

Quantum computers are a new type of machine that uses the strange behavior of subatomic particles to process information. Unlike ordinary computers, which store data as bits that are either zero or one, quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, that can exist in several states at once. In theory, this allows them to solve certain kinds of problems much faster than conventional machines. Although the technology is still in its early stages, major technology companies and governments are investing heavily in its development.

The potential applications are wide-ranging. Quantum computers could help scientists design new medicines by simulating how molecules interact, and they might improve the efficiency of batteries and fertilizers. Financial institutions are also interested in using them to analyze risk and optimize investment portfolios. Some experts believe that the most important application may be in cryptography, since quantum computers could eventually break many of the codes that currently protect online banking and private communications.

However, building a practical quantum computer remains extremely difficult. Qubits are highly sensitive to heat, vibration, and electromagnetic interference, so the machines must be kept at temperatures close to absolute zero. Errors occur frequently, and correcting them requires many additional qubits. For these reasons, most current machines are used only for research. Experts predict that it may take many years before quantum computers can outperform conventional systems on useful tasks, but the race to develop them has already begun.

Ghost kitchens, also called virtual kitchens or cloud kitchens, are restaurant facilities that prepare food only for delivery. They have no dining area and do not serve customers directly. Instead, several brands may share one kitchen, with each brand offering its own menu through food delivery apps. The model has grown rapidly in cities where rents are high and many customers order meals at home. Some investors see it as a way for restaurant companies to test new dishes without opening a full store.

The advantages for operators are clear. Because a ghost kitchen does not need a storefront or seating area, its owners can spend less on rent, furniture, and staff who manage the dining room. Kitchens can also be located near areas with many delivery customers, which helps to reduce delivery times. In addition, a single facility can host several brands, so the cost of equipment is spread across more products. Some owners say that this flexibility allows them to respond quickly to changes in consumer tastes.

However, the business model has drawn criticism. Customers who order from ghost kitchens often cannot see where their food is prepared, which can make it difficult to judge hygiene standards or the quality of ingredients. Restaurants with physical stores have also complained that virtual brands with similar menus compete unfairly for the same customers. Moreover, the business depends heavily on delivery platforms, which charge high commissions. Many analysts believe that the sector will need stricter rules and more transparent labeling before it can grow further.

Mindfulness, a practice that involves paying close attention to the present moment without judgment, has been introduced into schools in many countries. Typical programs include breathing exercises, short periods of silent reflection, and lessons on how to recognize and manage strong emotions. Some schools have made these activities part of the daily timetable, while others offer them as optional clubs. The idea is that children who learn these skills at a young age may be better able to cope with stress in later life.

Research on these programs has produced some encouraging results. Several studies have reported that students who took part in mindfulness training showed improvements in concentration, and some teachers say that their classrooms have become calmer. Participants have also reported feeling less anxious during exams. Supporters argue that such programs can be especially valuable for students who face difficult situations at home, because they give young people a simple method for calming themselves when they feel overwhelmed.

Critics, however, question whether the benefits are as large as advertised. Many studies are small or short, and it is unclear whether the effects last after the program ends. Some educators also worry that schools are being asked to take on responsibilities that belong to families or health professionals. In addition, teachers who are already busy may not have the training needed to lead such sessions effectively. For these reasons, many researchers believe that more rigorous studies are needed before mindfulness becomes a standard part of education.

topic: Traditional crafts and the shortage of successors
passage:
Traditional crafts such as pottery, lacquerware, and woven textiles have been passed down in Japan for centuries. Many of these skills were developed in specific regions, where local materials and climate shaped the techniques used by artisans. Today, however, many craftspeople are approaching retirement without anyone to take over their workshops. The number of people who train as apprentices has fallen sharply, and some traditional techniques are at risk of disappearing completely.

Several measures have been introduced to address this problem. Local governments offer subsidies to apprentices, and some workshops have opened training programs for people who have no family background in the craft. Others have begun selling their products online, which allows them to reach customers around the world and earn enough income to support a new generation of artisans. Museums and universities have also become involved, recording techniques on film and collaborating with designers to create products suited to modern homes.

Nevertheless, the work is demanding and often poorly paid. Learning a craft can take many years, and young people may find it hard to earn a living while they are still developing their skills. Some artisans are reluctant to share their methods with outsiders, fearing that their knowledge will be copied or that they will lose their identity. In addition, changes in lifestyle have reduced demand for many traditional products. Experts agree that the future of these crafts depends on finding a balance between preserving tradition and making the work sustainable for those who choose it.

Forest bathing, or shinrin-yoku, is a practice that began in Japan in the 1980s as a way to encourage people to spend time in forests. Rather than exercising strenuously, participants walk slowly among the trees, pay attention to the sounds and smells around them, and breathe deeply. The Japanese government promoted the idea as a way to reduce stress and to help people reconnect with nature. Today, forest bathing has spread to many countries, and guided programs are offered in national parks and private reserves.

A number of studies have suggested that the practice has health benefits. Some researchers have reported lower blood pressure and reduced levels of stress hormones among participants after a walk in the forest. Others have found that the trees release natural compounds into the air, which may support the immune system. Forest bathing is also accessible to a wide range of people, since it requires little equipment and does not demand high levels of fitness. Some doctors now recommend it as a complement to other forms of treatment for anxiety and depression.

However, the scientific evidence is still limited. Many studies are small, and it is difficult to separate the effects of the forest from those of walking itself or from the feeling of relaxation that comes from taking a break. Access is also uneven, since many people live in cities far from green areas. In addition, forests can be crowded during holidays, which may reduce the calm atmosphere that makes them attractive. Experts say that more research is needed to confirm the benefits and to determine which groups of people will benefit most.

Universal basic income, or UBI, is a proposal in which every citizen receives a regular payment from the government regardless of their income or employment status. In recent years, several countries and regions have carried out small-scale trials of the idea. Participants in these experiments have typically received a fixed monthly sum without conditions, and researchers have tracked how their work, health, and spending habits changed over time. The results have attracted attention from policymakers who are searching for new ways to support households.

Supporters argue that a basic income could provide security in an economy where jobs are increasingly unstable. Because people would no longer have to accept any job to survive, they might be able to pursue further education, care for family members, or start small businesses. Some trial participants reported lower levels of stress and greater confidence in their future. Advocates also claim that the system would be simpler to administer than the many separate benefits that governments currently provide, since fewer forms and eligibility checks would be needed.

Critics, however, point out that the cost of such a scheme would be very high. Funding a payment for every citizen would require either large tax increases or major cuts to existing public services. Some economists also worry that a guaranteed income might discourage people from working, although the trial results on this point are mixed. In addition, the most vulnerable groups, such as people with disabilities, may need extra support that a flat payment cannot provide. For these reasons, the debate over whether to adopt a basic income is likely to continue for years.

Coastal ecosystems such as mangrove forests, salt marshes, and seagrass beds are known as blue carbon habitats because they store large amounts of carbon in their roots and in the soil beneath them. Per hectare, these habitats can absorb carbon dioxide faster than many forests on land. However, when coastal wetlands are drained or filled in for construction, the stored carbon can be released back into the air, contributing to climate change. Losing these habitats also reduces the protection they offer against storms and rising seas.

Efforts to protect and restore these habitats have expanded in recent years. Some countries have begun replanting mangroves along their shores, and local communities have set up protected zones where fishing and development are restricted. Restoration projects can also provide income for local residents, who may be employed in planting, monitoring, and tourism. Some governments are exploring ways to sell carbon credits generated by healthy wetlands, which would give landowners a financial reason to conserve them.

Nevertheless, restoring coastal ecosystems is a complicated task. Many projects fail because the young plants are damaged by strong waves or because the local conditions for growth were not properly assessed. Measuring the amount of carbon stored in these habitats is also difficult, which makes it hard to prove the value of carbon credits. In addition, land along coasts is often valuable for ports, housing, and farming, so conservation projects may face strong opposition from businesses and residents. Experts emphasize that long-term planning and cooperation among all stakeholders are essential.

Lithium-ion batteries power a wide range of products, from smartphones to electric cars. As the number of electric vehicles on the road increases, the amount of used batteries is expected to rise sharply over the next decade. Many of these batteries still contain valuable metals such as lithium, cobalt, and nickel, which are costly to mine and refine. Recycling them could reduce the need for new mining and lower the environmental damage caused by extraction. For this reason, governments and companies have begun to develop systems for collecting and processing used batteries.

Several recycling technologies are now being tested. Some companies use heat to separate the metals from other materials, while others dissolve the battery components in chemicals and then recover the metals in a purer form. A newer approach involves taking batteries apart by hand and reusing their parts, which may be more efficient for batteries that are still in good condition. Some automakers have also started using recycled materials in their new batteries, which lowers their dependence on imported raw materials.

However, the process is not without problems. Batteries can catch fire if they are damaged during collection or transport, which makes handling them dangerous. The recycling plants themselves require large investments, and it is not always profitable to process batteries when metal prices are low. Moreover, many used batteries are still discarded in household waste because consumers do not know where to take them. Experts argue that clear regulations, safer transport methods, and better public awareness will be needed before battery recycling can become a truly sustainable industry.

Surge pricing, a system in which the cost of a service rises when demand is high, is widely used by ride-sharing companies, hotels, and airlines. Under this approach, prices are adjusted automatically in response to changes in supply and demand. For example, a taxi fare may increase during a heavy rainstorm, when many people are looking for a ride and fewer drivers are available. Companies argue that the system helps to balance demand with the resources they have, and it can encourage more drivers or sellers to offer their services when they are most needed.

The approach has several advantages for businesses. Revenue can increase during busy periods, and companies can use the extra income to cover the costs of operating at peak times. Some economists also argue that rising prices help to allocate scarce goods more efficiently, since those who need a service most urgently are more willing to pay for it. In addition, the system can reduce waiting times by encouraging some customers to choose a different time or place.

Nevertheless, many customers view surge pricing as unfair. People who are forced to pay high prices during emergencies or holidays may feel that they are being taken advantage of. Some governments have tried to limit the practice, especially for essential services such as transportation during natural disasters. There is also concern that automated pricing systems may be difficult for consumers to understand, which can damage trust between companies and their customers. As a result, businesses must balance the financial benefits of surge pricing against the risk of losing loyal customers.

Peer tutoring is a learning method in which students teach or help other students. In many schools, it has traditionally been used to support students who struggle with particular subjects, but it is now being used more widely. In some programs, older students guide younger ones, while in others, students with different strengths exchange roles. Teachers often arrange these pairs carefully so that both students benefit from the interaction.

Research suggests that peer tutoring can bring benefits to both sides. Tutors often gain a deeper understanding of a subject because explaining ideas to others requires them to organize their knowledge clearly. Students who receive help may feel more comfortable asking questions than they would with a teacher, since a classmate can seem less intimidating. Some schools have also reported improvements in attendance and in students' confidence, as well as stronger relationships among pupils from different backgrounds.

However, peer tutoring does not work well in every situation. Tutors may lack the knowledge or patience needed to explain difficult material, and they may give incorrect information without realizing it. Some students feel embarrassed when they are paired with a classmate who is younger or who has a lower level of ability. In addition, the program requires careful supervision and training, which takes time away from teachers' other responsibilities. For these reasons, most educators see peer tutoring as a useful supplement to classroom teaching rather than a replacement for it.

Vinyl records, which were once replaced by compact discs and then by digital music, have made an unexpected comeback in recent years. Sales of records have risen steadily in many countries, and some record stores report that young customers now make up a large share of their buyers. Many people who grew up with streaming services say that they are drawn to the physical nature of records, such as the large cover art and the ritual of placing a needle on the disc. The format has become a popular choice for collectors and music lovers alike.

The revival has brought several benefits to the music industry. Independent artists who release their work on vinyl can earn more money per copy than from streaming, where royalties are often very small. Limited editions and colored records have also encouraged fans to buy albums they might otherwise have listened to only online. In addition, the renewed interest has helped to keep small record shops and pressing plants in business, which in turn supports local music communities.

However, the boom has created some difficulties. The production of records is slow and expensive, and factories have struggled to meet demand, which has led to long waiting times for new releases. Environmental groups also point out that vinyl is made from petroleum-based plastic, so its production has a considerable carbon footprint. Some critics argue that the trend is driven more by nostalgia and fashion than by a genuine change in how people listen to music. Whether the interest will last beyond the current generation remains an open question.
